prompt.context: Our client is the North Australian Pastoral Company (NAPCO). NAPCO is a 143-year-old agriculture enterprise that is one of the leading companies in the space in Australia. They operate 13 cattle stations in Queensland and Northern Territory. Cattle stations are large cattle farms or ranches that raise cattle for slaughter. NAPCO's cattle stations cover over 60,000 square kilometers and they manage over 200,000 head of cattle. Their largest station is Alexandria Station in Northern Territory that is over 16,000 square kilometers and supports herds of over 55,000 head. 10,000 head are due to be delivered to Darwin next month, but due to heavy flooding in Northern Territory, the train tracks they normally use to deliver their mature cattle from Alexandria Station to market in Darwin are inaccessible and we will be unable to repair the damage until the end of the wet season next April.
prompt.question: What factors would you consider in deciding how to advise NAPCO how to deliver the cattle?

clarifying_info.q: What is the terrain between Alexandria Station and Darwin?
clarifying_info.a: There is a variety of terrain including wetlands and marshes, but mostly rolling flatlands.

exhibits.title: Cattle Drive Routes
exhibits.shows: A table showing two possible cattle drive routes (Coorabulka Route and Boomarra Route), each with three pace options (15, 30, and 50 km/day) and the corresponding daily grass consumption per head at each pace. A note states cattle lose 1kg every day on a cattle drive regardless of grass intake.

data.note: Cattle lose 1kg every day on a cattle drive, regardless of grass intake

framework: 1. Profitability: a) Revenues — 10k cattle, price per head/pound; b) Costs — transport, fuel, feed, SG&A

2. Delivery: a) Location — how far is Darwin, where else can we take them; b) Method — train (unflooded stations), plane (landing strips), trucks (transport of 10k cattle), cattle drive (best option if train is out); c) Timing — contract pricing, late fees, insurance
3. Risks: a) Lost animals; b) Opportunity cost for labor; c) Damaged relationships — buyers, shippers, brokers

questions.prompt: NAPCO has decided to revive an old practice and drive the cattle to another station where they can be loaded onto trains and delivered to Darwin. The station manager has identified two stations: Coorabulka Station or Boomarra Station. What factors should NAPCO consider when comparing these options?
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover: 1) Profitability — selling price per head/pound, feed costs (what cattle eat, how much per day, cost per bushel), water availability given flooding, cost of extra labor and opportunity cost; 2) Operations — capability to drive cattle, security of route, lost cattle risk, cattle health on the drive, horses vs trucks, supply points (water, food, bedding) for cattle and drovers.

questions.prompt: The station manager has given details on the routes. Route A follows the Georgina River 600 km southeast to Coorabulka Station. Route B is 300 km due east to Boomarra Station. He also passed along information on the effects of driving a herd on the cattle (Exhibit 1). Which route and pace should NAPCO take to minimize revenue loss from weight loss?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use Exhibit 1 to calculate weight lost per head for each route/pace combination. Key clarifying info: cattle require 3% of their mature weight in grass feed per day (500 kg * 3% = 15 kg/day needed); cattle lose half the unreplaced weight every day; all cattle are Alexandria Composite sold by the pound at $800 USD per head at mature weight; mature slaughter weight = 500 kg; price per kg = $800/500 = $1.60. Calculate net kg lost per day = 1 (base loss) + (grass required - grass eaten)/2, then multiply by days traveled to get total weight lost per head, then total revenue lost.

math.setup: Price per kg = $800 / 500 kg = $1.60/kg. Net kg lost per day = 1 + (15 - grass_eaten) / 2. Days = distance / pace. Total revenue lost = net_kg_lost_per_day * days * $1.60 * 10,000 cattle.
steps: Coorabulka (600 km), pace 15 km/day: net loss/day = 1 + (15-15)/2 = 1 kg/day; days = 40; total weight lost/head = 40 kg; lost rev/head = 40 * 1.60 = $64; total = $64 * 10,000 = $640k
Coorabulka (600 km), pace 30 km/day: net loss/day = 1 + (15-10)/2 = 3.5 kg/day; days = 20; total = 3.5*20*1.60*10,000 = $1.12m
Coorabulka (600 km), pace 50 km/day: net loss/day = 1 + (15-8)/2 = 4.5 kg/day; days = 12; total = 4.5*12*1.60*10,000 = $870k
Boomarra (300 km), pace 15 km/day: net loss/day = 1 + (15-15)/2 = 1 kg/day; days = 20; total = 1*20*1.60*10,000 = $320k
Boomarra (300 km), pace 30 km/day: net loss/day = 1 + (15-6)/2 = 5.5 kg/day; days = 10; total = 5.5*10*1.60*10,000 = $880k
Boomarra (300 km), pace 50 km/day: net loss/day = 1 + (15-3)/2 = 7 kg/day; days = 6; total = 7*6*1.60*10,000 = $670k
Minimum revenue loss from weight alone: Boomarra at 15 km/day = $320k (Coorabulka at 15 km/day = $640k is next best)
math.answer: To minimize weight-loss revenue loss alone, Boomarra at 15 km/day ($320k) is best. Coorabulka at 15 km/day costs $640k.

questions.prompt: The station manager says NAPCO will need to hire 20 aboriginal Warlpiri drovers at $100/day each. NAPCO will also lose 0.5% of cattle on the Coorabulka route and 1% of cattle on the Boomarra route. Incorporating labor costs and cattle losses, which route and pace should NAPCO take?
questions.guidance: Add labor costs (20 drovers * $100/day * number of days) and lost cattle value (% lost * 10,000 head * $800/head) to the weight-loss revenue figures. Compare total cost across all options. The important part is the rationale — e.g., if both routes cost nearly the same, recommend the option that is better for animal welfare (slower pace). Warn against stressing cattle to save a trivial amount (e.g., 50 km/day to save $480 looks bad publicly).

math.setup: Labor cost = 20 drovers * $100/day * days. Lost cattle value = loss_rate * 10,000 * $800. Total cost = weight loss revenue + labor + lost cattle.
steps: Coorabulka at 15 km/day: weight loss = $640k; labor = 20*100*40 = $80k; lost cattle = 0.5%*10,000*$800 = $40k (500*1.6*50 shown as $37k in casebook using weight-adjusted price); total ≈ $757k

Boomarra at 15 km/day: weight loss = $320k (from exhibit solution) — NOTE: casebook uses 15km/day for Boomarra with weight loss recalculated as $460 lost weight context; labor = 20*100*20 = $40k (or $12k at faster pace); lost cattle = 1%*10,000*$800 = $80k (casebook shows 458*1.6*100=$73k using weight-adjusted); total ≈ $757k
Both routes end up costing nearly the same (~$757k each at their respective optimal paces).
math.answer: Both routes cost approximately $757k. Since total cost is nearly equal, recommend the route and pace that treats animals better and avoids reputational risk from driving cattle at 50 km/day for marginal savings.

recommendation: Both the Coorabulka and Boomarra routes cost approximately $757k when factoring in weight loss revenue, labor, and lost cattle — making them effectively equivalent on cost.

Recommend Coorabulka Route at 15 km/day as it minimizes animal stress; driving cattle at faster paces (50 km/day) saves negligible amounts while risking reputational damage and animal welfare concerns.
risks: Reputational risk if word spreads that NAPCO drives cattle at extreme pace for trivial savings
Animal welfare and herd health deterioration at high pace (50 km/day)
Further cattle losses from terrain hazards (wetlands, marshes) along the route
Relationship damage with buyers, shippers, or brokers if delivery is delayed or cattle arrive underweight
next_steps: Confirm drovers availability and finalize contracts with Warlpiri drovers
Identify and pre-position supply points (water, food, bedding) along the chosen route
Communicate expected delivery timeline to Darwin buyers and renegotiate any penalty clauses if needed
Monitor flooding levels to assess whether train repairs can be expedited before April
